Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience

vignette: As she walked through the hospital corridors, Leila couldn't shake off the feeling of unease that had been her constant companion for months. It started after a particularly difficult delivery, when one of the doctors had brushed against her in a way that felt too familiar, too invasive. The discomfort was palpable, like a weight on her skin, and it lingered long after the shift ended. Leila tried to push it aside, but it only seemed to intensify as she went about her daily routine as a midwife. She began to feel self-conscious, aware of every glance, every movement that might draw attention to herself. Patients would smile at her, and she'd force a smile back, all the while wondering if they could see right through her, sense the fear that had taken up residence in her chest. Leila's husband, Tom, noticed the change too - she'd become withdrawn, hesitant to go out or socialize with friends. He attributed it to stress, but Leila knew better. It started after the rape, two years ago. The memory still lingered, a constant presence that threatened to overwhelm her at any moment. She recalled the smell of burnt food wafting from the kitchen, the way it had seared itself into her brain as she lay helpless on the floor. Now, whenever she caught a whiff of something similar - toast burning in the toaster, a candle flame flickering too close - Leila's heart would start racing, her senses going on high alert. She began to listen for sounds that might signal someone was entering their home, even when Tom was with her. The creak of a floorboard, a rustle outside - each noise became a potential threat, and she'd tense up, ready to spring into action. Leila knew it was irrational, but the fear had taken hold, spreading its tendrils deep into her psyche. As she studied people's faces and body language, searching for signs of malice or intent, Leila realized that this hypervigilance came at a cost. Patients began to notice her distraction, her hesitation to connect with them on a deeper level. Her colleagues whispered about her being "off" - a midwife who was normally so warm and nurturing now seemed remote, detached. Leila's physical reactions grew more pronounced too - a strong reaction whenever something reminded her of that fateful night. A man's raised voice, the way a stranger touched her arm in passing - each incident sent her reeling back into that dark space where terror held sway. Her sleep was fitful, haunted by nightmares and flashbacks. As she struggled to keep up with her demanding job, Leila realized that this cycle of fear had to break. The discomfort, the self-consciousness, the constant threat monitoring - it all fed back into itself, a vicious loop that left her breathless and exhausted. With a deep sigh, she made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to untangle the web of emotions that had taken over her life. Tom asked what had finally prompted her to seek help, and Leila's voice was barely above a whisper: "I just want to be able to touch my patients without flinching. I want to look at people without seeing monsters." The fear still lingered, but with it came a glimmer of determination - she would learn to confront this terror head-on, no matter how daunting the task seemed.
